title: Gather the requirements
subtitle: The Stage 1 lesson: the six parts of a requirements document, the questions that fill each part, and how to check the document is ready.

slides.narration: Here is a request for a new application. It is two sentences long. We need a way to text our users when something changes, such as an office closure. Staff should be able to pick a group and schedule the message.
By the end of Stage 1, those two sentences had become eight written requirements. Four of them came from questions about things the request never mentioned.

This lesson covers Stage 1 of the Core Build Starter Guide: gathering the requirements. You will learn the six parts of a requirements document, the questions that fill each part, and how to check that the document is ready for Stage 2.
Stage 1 is the first of nine stages, and it has no code. Its output is one written document: the requirements.
Every later stage takes its input from that document. Stage 2 picks tools to meet it. Stage 7 designs the database from it. Stage 8 tests against the load numbers in it.
Throughout the lesson we use one example, an application called User Notices. Staff sign in, browse a list of users, edit a user's details, and schedule text messages to groups of users.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: The requirements document has six parts. Here they are, one at a time.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: Part 1 is screens: what a user does, screen by screen. Stage 6 turns each screen into a page and a route, and Stage 9 gives each screen a test owner.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: Part 2 is stored data. Stage 7 turns it into tables.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: Part 3 is external services, the systems outside the application. Stage 2 picks the API approach from it, and Stage 8 keeps calls under each service's limits.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: Part 4 is load. Stage 8 tests the application at that load.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: Part 5 is constraints, the rules you did not choose. A constraint overrides a default tool in Stage 2. Part 6 is the deployment target, where the application will run. Stages 8 and 9 build for it.

slides.chapter: The six parts of a requirements document
slides.narration: If a part is left empty, the stages that read it start without their input. Leave out load, and Stage 8 has nothing to test against.

Stage 1 runs in six steps. Step 1: record the request exactly as it was given, who asked, and the problem it solves. Step 2: find the people. That means the users, the data owner, and whoever runs the servers.
Step 3: walk through the work with each kind of user. Step 4: draft the six parts. Anything you don't know goes in as an open question, with the name of the person who can answer it.

Step 5: read the draft back to the requester and the users, screen by screen, and ask what is missing or wrong. Any gap sends you back to step 3. Steps 3, 4 and 5 repeat until the read-back finds nothing missing.
Step 6: the requester agrees the document, and you give it a version number and a date. Stage 2 starts from that version.

Step 3 is where most of the material comes from. Talk to each kind of user separately. Staff who send notices and the administrator who creates staff accounts use different screens. Start by asking them to show you how they do the task today, from the start.

Then keep asking. What happens next? What do you look at before you decide? What goes wrong, and what do you do then? How often do you do this, and when is it busiest? Who else needs to see or approve it? And what should the application never do?
Also ask to see the tools they use now: spreadsheets, emails, paper forms. Every column or form field is a candidate for the stored data list.
Part 1 lists every screen a user sees. For each one, write what the user does on it, the data it shows or accepts, and whether it is needed at launch or later.
To find the screens, follow a task from start to end. Each place the user looks at or types into is a candidate. Then follow the verbs: list, open, create, edit, delete, search, send.
Check that every thing you store can be created, viewed, changed and removed somewhere. Then add the edge cases: signing in, a forgotten password, an empty list, and a user without permission.
Quick check. Here is the Notice history screen. Is Send now a screen of its own, or an action? Decide before the answer appears.
Send now is an action. A screen shows its own information or has its own form. An action is a button or control on a screen. Notice history is the screen, and Send now is a button on it.
Next, map how the screens connect. For User Notices, Sign in leads to the Users list and to Notice history, through the navigation bar.
The Users list opens User detail, where staff view and edit one user.

Notice history shows every notice with its status and a Send now action. It leads to New notice, where staff write a notice, pick a group, and set a send time. Saving the notice returns to Notice history.
A chat panel is marked for later, after launch. On your own map, a screen that no arrow reaches is a gap. A paper sketch is enough. Stage 6 decides the layout.
Part 2 lists everything the application stores, reads or logs, grouped by the thing it describes. You are not designing tables yet. Stage 7 does that.
Read the values off your screens. The New notice screen gives you a notice's text, its group, and its send time. Each value goes under the thing it describes, here a notice.

For each thing, ask who creates it, who changes it, whether it can be deleted, and how long it is kept. Ask what must be logged, because a log is stored data and needs a table. And mark sensitive data, such as phone numbers and passwords.
Count the records, today and per month. And note any files, because files go to object storage, not the database.
User Notices has five things: staff accounts, users, groups, notices, and a send record for every message.

Two answers were unknown: who maintains groups, and how many notices go out each month. Both are written as open questions. A guessed number looks the same as a real one to the person who reads it in Stage 7.
Part 3 lists every system outside the application that it calls, or that calls it.

For each one, ask which direction the calls go. Ask what is sent, and what comes back. Ask how often, and whether calls come in bursts. Ask what limits the service sets, such as requests per second. Ask who owns the account and the key, what happens when the service is down, and whether there is a test account.
User Notices has one external service, an SMS provider. The application calls it once per message, sends a phone number and the text, and stores the message ID that comes back.

One notice can mean 5,000 calls at its send time. The provider has a rate limit, and Stage 8 keeps the application under it. What happens when the provider is down, and whether there is a test account, are open questions.
Part 4 records load as two separate numbers.
The first is registered users: the accounts that can sign in. User Notices has 150 staff accounts.

The second is concurrent requests: how many requests the backend is handling at the same moment, at the busiest time. For User Notices, that is at most 40. Stage 8 tests at this second number, not the first.
Quick check. The application also holds 60,000 user records. Do they count as load?
No. Those people receive text messages, but they never sign in. They add data, not load.
Often nobody can give you the concurrent number, so you estimate it and record that it is an estimate. Take an application with 100,000 registered users.
Assume 3 percent are online at the busiest time. That is 3,000 people.
If each one makes about 2 requests a minute, that is 6,000 requests a minute, or 100 requests a second.
If each request takes about half a second, the backend is handling 50 requests at the same moment. So 100,000 registered users can mean 50 concurrent requests.
Replace each assumption with a real figure when you can get one, from logs, from the busiest shift, or from your step 3 notes. And record the number expected in a year as well.

Also record every burst. A burst is a known event that sends many requests or jobs at once, even when daily traffic is light. Ask about scheduled bulk sends, nightly jobs, month end, the start of a shift, and deadlines.
User Notices has one burst. When a notice reaches its send time, it can send up to 5,000 messages at once. Stage 8 moves that work out of the request and onto a queue.

slides.chapter: Parts 5 and 6: Constraints and deployment target
slides.narration: Part 5 records the rules the application must follow that you did not choose. Part 6 records where the application will run.

slides.chapter: Parts 5 and 6: Constraints and deployment target
slides.narration: Ask whether the organization mandates a language, framework or database, and which licenses it already holds. Ask where data may be stored and whether any of it is personal data. Ask who may sign in, which roles exist, and which accessibility standard applies. For the target, ask whether it is a cloud provider or the organization's own servers, and how many environments.

slides.chapter: Parts 5 and 6: Constraints and deployment target
slides.narration: These answers change later stages. For User Notices, data must stay on the organization's own servers, with no cloud provider. So Stage 2 cannot use cloud storage, and Stage 9 deploys to two Linux servers, one live and one sandbox.

slides.chapter: Parts 5 and 6: Constraints and deployment target
slides.narration: A mandated database discovered at deployment means Stages 2, 3 and 7 are done again. That is why these questions are asked in Stage 1.
Now put it together. Here is the User Notices request again. Each phrase leads to a question.

Text our users: who receives the messages, and do they sign in? That gives 60,000 people on record who never sign in, and 150 staff accounts who do. Which service sends the messages? The SMS provider.
Pick a group: how many users are in the largest group? Up to 5,000. Schedule the message: can staff see a scheduled notice and send it early? That gives the Notice history screen with Send now.
That is four requirements from the request itself. Before the next slide, think of something User Notices needs that the request never mentioned.

Four questions found the rest. Do you need a record of what was sent to whom? Do staff change user details? How many staff use it at the busiest moment? And where may the data be stored? Those produced the send log, the User detail screen, the 40 concurrent requests, and the two servers.

Six questions were still open when the requirements were agreed, and none of them holds up Stage 2. Each one is written down with the person who can answer it and the stage that needs the answer: the SMS test account by Stage 5, the sending roles and group upkeep by Stage 6, monthly volume and record keeping by Stage 7, the outage plan by Stage 8, and the accessibility standard by Stage 9.
Next, spot the mistake. Each weak requirement appears first, as it is often written. Number one: build it in React with MongoDB.
The tool was chosen before the requirements. Write what the application needs instead, and leave tools to Stage 2.
Number two: 100,000 users.
Load is written as one number. Write registered users and concurrent requests separately.
Number three: light traffic during the day.
A burst is left out. Light traffic during the day can still include 5,000 messages at one send time.
Number four: send records are kept for one year.
This is a guess written as a fact. If nobody has confirmed it, it is an open question with an owner.
Number five: a draft sent by email.
The requirements were never read back. A draft sent by email is not agreement. Read it back in a meeting, and record the version and the date it was agreed.
Now a quick sort. For each statement, pick the part of the requirements document it belongs in. First: messages go only to users who have opted in.
Part 5, constraints. It is a privacy rule the application must follow. The opt-in value itself is stored data, in Part 2.
Next: a forgotten password is reset through a link sent by email.
Part 3, external services. Sending email needs an email service outside the application.
Last: one notice can send up to 5,000 messages at its send time.
Part 4, load. It is a burst: many jobs at one moment, even when daily traffic is light.
Now try it yourself. A requester asks for a simple online diary. Members sign in, write entries, edit or delete old ones, and search their own entries for a word.

When asked, the requester says there are 2,000 members today, and 5,000 are expected in a year. Most writing happens in the evening, with up to 300 members online at once. Each online member makes about 2 requests a minute. Entries are private to their author. A forgotten password is reset by email. And data may be stored with a cloud provider in the same country.
Pause the video now and draft all six parts. Include the concurrent request estimate, using half a second per request.

Here is one possible answer. Screens: sign in, forgotten password, an entry list, an entry screen to write, view, edit and delete, search results, and an account screen. Stored data: members and their entries. External services: an email service for password reset links.

Load: 2,000 registered members. 300 online, times 2 requests a minute, divided by 60, times half a second, gives 5 concurrent requests. That rises to about 13 in a year. There are no scheduled bursts.

Constraints: entries are private to their author. Deployment target: a cloud provider in the same country, with a live environment and a sandbox. At about 5 concurrent requests, Stage 8 for this application is a load test and a decision table with most layers marked not needed.

Before you start Stage 2, check seven things. Every screen is listed, with who uses it and where it leads. Stored data is listed by thing, including logs, sensitive data and record counts. External services are listed with their volume, limits and account owner. Load is recorded as two numbers with their sources, plus every burst. Constraints and the deployment target are written down. Every open question has an owner and the stage that needs the answer. And the requester has agreed the document, with a version number and a date.

The workbook for this stage, linked in the description, has the requirements template, the load calculator, and the practice exercises. In the next lesson, Stage 2, you pick a tool for each layer of the application, starting from this document.
